key_concepts: [url]How to create procedural wall with blender geometry nodes^^https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b_vAUbQpHvI[/url]

content: Start with the default cube, adding a Geometry Nodes Modifier (Image 1).

Our brick wall will be following our curve. Give the Bézier Curve a Geometry Nodes modifier with a [k]Resample Curve[/k] node with the Mode set to Length and a Length of 0.2m (standard length of a brick and mortar joint) (Image 4). We need to bring the curve up to the height of our wall, so add a [k]Curve to Mesh[/k] node and then an [k]Extrude Mesh[/k] node with the Mode set to Edges to bring it out (Image 5). Our mesh is extruding in the normal direction for our curve, which is the y-axis; we need to convert this to the z-axis by adding in a [k]Vector[/k] node to isolate the Offset in the z-axis (Image 6). For the brick layout, we need each cell of the grid's height and width to be the same. We will do this by bringing in a constant Value for the [k]Resample Curve[/k]'s Length and the [k]Extrude Mesh[/k]'s Offset Scale (Image 7). This defines a row of bricks, but we will want several rows; add a [k]Duplicate Elements[/k] node which creates a new geometry with the specified elements from the input duplicated an arbitrary number of times (Image 8). The rows are duplicated, but they are all in the same position. Add in a [k]Set Position[/k] node and Offset each element by its Duplicate Index (Image 9). We see the rows offset by their index in each axis; isolate the offset with a [k]Combine XYZ[/k] node to just the z-axis (Image 10). The offset is still too much since it is 1 unit per row; we will adjust this with a [k]Multiply[/k] node using the constant Value we defined earlier (Image 11). If we look at the Spreadsheet, there are 160 vertices, or 40 per row (Image 12). That is due to overlapping vertices. we can fix this with a [k]Merge by Distance[/k] node (Image 13). We have our grid layout, now we need to place a brick on each grid face. Add a [k]Mesh to Points[/k] node which will visualize each location a brick should go (Image 14). With our points we can add brick instances on each one, but first we need our instance.

Add a Cube to the scene and start editing (Image 15). Move the cube up 1m so the origin point is at the bottom (Image 16). In Object Mode, change the dimensions to a standard brick size (Image 17). [k]Ctrl-A,S[/k] to apply the scale and add a Bevel Modifier (Image 18). Rename the mesh in the Outliner and hide it (Image 19).

Back to the curve, at this point, we have created a grid of squares that are 0.2m x 0.2m (Image 20). We need to update the row height to use our fixed brick height or 0.07m. Bring in a constant [k]Value[/k] node set to the right height and connect it to the [k]Extrude Mesh[/k]'s Offset Scale and the [k]Multiply[/k] node used to set each row's Z offset (Image 21).

Bring the brick mesh into the network and add it as instances on the center point of all grid faces (Image 22). If we look at it, the bricks do not follow the curve of the wall (Image 23). We need to capture the curve's tangent so that we can use that to align the brick's rotation to it. First, add a [k]Store Named Attribute[/k] and [k]Curve Tangent[/k] node to read that information (Image 24). The [k]Store Named Attribute[/k] allows us to store the result of a field on the geometry which in this case we are reading the direction of the curve at each control point. Name our stored attribute 'tangent'; later if we bring in a [k]Named Attribute[/k] node to retrieve the data we can find it under that name (Image 25). Over at the [k]Instance on Points[/k] node, add a [k]Align Rotation to Vector[/k] node, set its Vector input to the 'tangent' attribute we created and connect the to the Rotation output to the [k]Instance on Points[/k] Rotation input (Image 26). If the rotation isn't correct, change the Axis property to see if one is a better match (Image 27).
